newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey in spat with Iran over expulsions.
newsitem.headline: Turkey in spat with Iran over expulsions.

text.p: Turkish-Iranian relations took on a sour note after Turkey expelled an Iranian consul for criticising a secularist army commander amid reports on Friday that Iran would retaliate by pushing out two Turkish envoys.

The bilateral unease comes at a time when Turkey's secularist military is putting pressure on the country's first Islamist-led government to steer clear of harming the 73-year-old republic's secular and democratic institutions.
The Turkish foreign ministry would not immediately confirm reports of two expulsions from Iran.
"We should be making a statement later," one official said.
But private ATV television quoted a ministry source as saying the pair would be recalled for consultations.
An Iranian newspaper published by the official news agency, IRNA, reported:

"Apparently Turkey's ambassador in Tehran and that country's consul-general in Orumiyeh will be expelled from Iran in retaliation for the Turkish government's action toward our country's ambassador," the daily said.
The squabbling may endanger a $23-billion gas deal signed between the two countries last year in defiance of Washington.
"In view of our energy needs, Iran is the most viable resource, but the political issue is another matter," energy ministry undersecretary Ugur Dogan told Reuters.

The two countries entered into a diplomatic row after Ankara protested to Tehran earlier this month about Iranian ambassador Mohammad Reza Bagheri for his comments in favour of Islamic law at an Islamist rally in the Ankara district of Sincan.
Tanks toured Sincan several days after the protest in an apparent warning to Islamists from the secularist army.
Turkey's generals are expected to warn the Islamist-right government over the Sincan affair and other Islamist incidents during a meeting with top ministers on Friday.
Tehran has withdrawn ambassador Bagheri, although MPs of the Islamist Welfare Party -- the senior coalition partner -- say the move is unrelated to the events surrounding the rally.
Erbakan worried secularist Turks and the West early in his eight-month tenure with overtures to Turkey's big eastern neighbour. He went to Tehran on his first major foreign visit.

Analysts say the irony of Erbakan presiding over the latest tensions demonstrates the impossibility of the two neighbours ever working with full trust and cooperation despite having the best bilateral ties of the region.
Iran is the one bordering country with which Turkey has maintained stable relations, but this does not dispel the phobia that Tehran is out to destabilise the secular state.

There is also the more concrete fear that separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas are getting support from Iran. Turkish security officials often say that the PKK attacks Turkish border posts from Iranian soil.
This issue most often splits the military and Welfare and lies at the heart of a series of spats that began in April after a Turkish hitman said he had been trained in Iran.

In the latest incident, Turkey on Thursday declared Iran's Erzurum chief consul Saeede Zare 'persona non grata' following his attack on a senior military commander for criticising Iran over its alleged support of guerrillas.

According to Anatolian news agency, Zare had accused the deputy chief of the Turkish armed forces, Cevik Bir, of "irresponsibility" for apparently describing Iran as a "terrorist" state. He has been asked to leave by the weekend.
